title: A Verdict for the Parish Revisited
premise: Marguerite Yarrow built her podcast 'A Verdict for the Parish' on the unsolved 1994 disappearance of altar boy Thomas Reeve in the coastal town of Bellhaven, careful to keep every source anonymous and herself invisible. When twin letters arrive—one confessing to the crime, the other promising 'more if you keep digging'—she realizes someone is using her show as a confessional, and that the statute of limitations on related obstruction charges expires in ninety days. As Marguerite peels back alibis woven by three families who protected each other for thirty years, she discovers her own late mother was the parish secretary who shredded the original evidence. In the end, Marguerite broadcasts the truth knowing it will destroy the man who raised her after her mother's death—the confessing letter-writer—and chooses justice over the only loyalty she has left.
about_author: Elodie Halloran is the pen name of a former court stenographer from the Maine coast who spent two decades transcribing small-town trials before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about communities that mistake silence for peace.

chapters.title: Twin Envelopes
chapters.summary: POV: Marguerite. Two letters arrive the same morning—one a detailed confession to Thomas Reeve's disappearance signed only 'The Sexton,' the other promising more secrets if she keeps digging. Marguerite, who has spent seven years keeping Bellhaven's secrets alphabetized rather than aired, feels both thrill and dread. Emotional beat: the hunter realizes she has become the hunted.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Silence
chapters.summary: POV: Marguerite. She reviews her private files on the case: three families, thirty years, alibis so tidy they feel rehearsed. Her producer pushes her to air the confession; Marguerite resists, sensing a trap. A visit to the retired sheriff yields one crack—his memory of a second boy seen near the churchyard that night. Emotional beat: unease deepening into obsession.

chapters.title: What the Sexton Knew
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Marguerite and an anonymous second-person voice implied to be the letter-writer. The Sexton watches her podcast downloads spike and mails a third letter containing a detail never made public: the color of Thomas's bike. Marguerite confirms it against a sealed police report, proving the writer was there. Emotional beat: vertigo—the confession is real, and so is the threat.

chapters.title: Three Families, One Roof
chapters.summary: POV: Marguerite. She interviews the descendants of the three families tied to the parish: the Reeve cousins, the deacon's son, and the Vances who owned the funeral home. Each alibi covers another like shingles. The deacon's son, drunk, lets slip that his father 'took care of the sexton's problem.' Emotional beat: the town's loyalty revealed as complicity.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Drawer
chapters.summary: POV: Marguerite. Sorting her late mother's belongings, she finds a parish key ring and a burned-edge photograph of her mother with the sexton, Aldous Wren—the kindly handyman who helped raise Marguerite after her mother died. A shredder receipt dated 1995 sits in the same drawer. Emotional beat: grief curdling into betrayal.

chapters.title: Ninety Days
chapters.summary: POV: Marguerite. A lawyer warns her that obstruction evidence she uncovers could implicate her mother posthumously and herself as a recipient of stolen records; the statute clock is running. Meanwhile the Sexton's fourth letter names a burial site under the old chapel annex. Marguerite must decide whether digging means becoming an accessory. Emotional beat: fear wearing the mask of duty.

chapters.title: The Annex Floor
chapters.summary: POV: Marguerite, with brief interludes from the Sexton's letters read aloud. With her producer filming secretly at night, they find disturbed ground beneath the annex—but someone has tipped off the diocese, and a crew arrives at dawn to pour concrete. They salvage a single button and soil samples. Emotional beat: triumph snatched at, then nearly buried.

chapters.title: Confession, Second Draft
chapters.summary: POV: Marguerite. Confronting Aldous Wren in his garden, she lays out the button, the photo, the shredded files. He admits he was there the night Thomas died—but claims he took the blame for someone else, and that her mother knew everything. The fifth letter arrives mid-conversation, hand-delivered: 'Ask her what she carried out.' Emotional beat: the ground giving way beneath every certainty.

chapters.title: The Statute and the Sermon
chapters.summary: POV: Marguerite. Records reveal her mother didn't shred evidence—she hid it, trading silence for protection from the deacon, whose assault of Thomas the sexton witnessed. The real killer died years ago; the surviving sin is the cover-up, expiring in days. Marguerite must choose: bury her mother's secret or broadcast it. Emotional beat: the scales tipping toward truth at terrible cost.

chapters.title: A Verdict, Delivered
chapters.summary: POV: Marguerite. On the final episode, she airs everything—the sexton's letters, the annex, her mother's hidden file—naming no living murderer but indicting the machinery of silence. Aldous turns himself in for obstruction; the parish annex is excavated; Thomas Reeve comes home. Marguerite, no longer invisible, signs her own name on air. Emotional beat: costly, hard-won peace.
